title: Red Flags in a Relationship (and Green Flags to Look For) — cv.cm
description: Red flags in a relationship: control, jealousy, isolation, lying, contempt and more, why each matters, green and yellow flags, and how to raise a concern.
h1: What are the red flags in a relationship?
answer: Red flags are behaviors that signal a risk of control, disrespect or abuse. The most serious are controlling who you see or what you do, jealousy presented as love, checking your phone, cutting you off from friends, lying, contempt, ignoring your "no", and anger that makes you afraid. Even one or two of these deserve attention. Fear is never a normal part of love.

sections.h: The main red flags and why they matter
body: These patterns apply to anyone, of any gender, in any kind of relationship. Some people search for 渣男 behaviors, the Chinese word for a man who plays with partners' feelings; the signs below cover that and more, and they are about behavior, not about men or women as groups.

head: Red flag
What it can look like
Why it matters
What to do next
rows: Control
Telling you what to wear, where to go, who to see; controlling money
Limits your freedom step by step
Name it once; if it continues, get outside support
Jealousy presented as love
"I only get angry because I love you so much"
Turns control into something that sounds romantic
Do not accept jealousy as proof of love
Isolating you
Criticizing your friends and family, sulking when you see them
Removes the people who would notice problems
Keep your friendships and tell someone you trust
Checking your phone
Reading messages, tracking location, demanding passwords
A sign of control and lack of trust
You can say no; privacy is normal in healthy couples
Lying
Repeated lies about where they were, money, other partners
Trust cannot grow on false information
Ask directly; repeated lying is a serious warning
Contempt
Mocking, eye-rolling, name-calling, sarcasm about who you are
Gottman's research names contempt the strongest predictor of divorce
Ask for respect; contempt that continues is a dealbreaker
Hot and cold
Very loving, then cold or cruel, with no clear reason
Keeps you anxious and working to win them back
Watch the pattern over weeks; see the love bombing article
No respect for "no"
Pressure after you refuse, including about sex
Consent is the base of a safe relationship
Hold your "no"; this is a serious sign
Anger you fear
Shouting, breaking things, threats, blocking the door
Fear means safety is at risk
Make a safety plan and contact a support service
Blame
Every problem is your fault; they never apologize
You start doubting yourself
Reality-check with a friend; see the gaslighting article

body: Domestic abuse services in many countries list very similar signs. The US National Domestic Violence Hotline notes that even one or two of these behaviors can be a red flag.

sections.h: Green flags: what a healthy relationship looks like
body: Knowing what good looks like makes red flags easier to see. Green flags include:

ul: They respect your "no" the first time, without sulking or punishing you.
They are glad you have friends, family and interests of your own.
Their words and actions match. They do what they say they will do.
They can disagree without insults and can say "I'm sorry, I was wrong".
You feel safe to tell them how you feel, including when you are upset with them.
They are curious about your life and remember what matters to you.
They respond to small moments of connection, like your story about your day.
Trust does not depend on checking each other's phones.
The relationship moves at a pace you both are comfortable with.

body: The Gottman Institute's research on bids for connection found that couples who stayed together turned toward each other's small attempts at connection much more often than couples who later divorced. Everyday kindness is a strong green flag.

sections.h: Yellow flags: things that need a conversation
body: Some behaviors are not dangerous on their own but deserve a calm talk. How the person responds to that talk tells you a lot.

head: Yellow flag
Possible reasons
A way to raise it
rows: Often late or cancels plans
Busy life, poor planning, or low priority
"When plans change last minute, I feel unimportant. Can we plan things we can both keep?"
Vague about the relationship
Unsure, or keeping options open
"I'd like to know where we're heading. What are you looking for?"
Drinks a lot
Stress, social habits, or a real problem
"I've noticed you drink more when we go out. It worries me."
Talks badly about every ex
Real hurt, or a habit of blaming others
"What do you think you'd do differently next time?"
Slow to reply to messages
Different chat habits or work
"I'm someone who likes a quick reply when we're making plans. What works for you?"
Avoids meeting your friends
Shyness, or wanting you to themselves
"It matters to me that you meet my friends. Could we do something small?"

body.note: A yellow flag becomes red if the person reacts to a gentle question with anger, contempt or punishment.

body: If you feel safe with the person, a direct conversation is usually the best next step. If you feel afraid, skip this and go to the help section below.

ol: Pick a calm moment, not in the middle of a fight or by message late at night.
Describe one specific behavior, not their character: "Last week you read my messages while I was in the shower."
Say how it affected you: "I felt watched and it hurt my trust."
Say what you need: "I need my phone to be private. If you are worried about something, please ask me."
Listen to their answer. Do they get curious and take responsibility, or do they blame you?
Watch the following weeks. Change shows in actions, not only in promises.

body: Each person decides their own dealbreakers, but some patterns should be treated as reasons to leave or to get support to leave:

ul: Any physical violence, including pushing, grabbing or throwing things at you.
Sexual pressure or sex without clear consent.
Threats to hurt you, your family, your pets, or themselves if you leave.
Ongoing control of your money, phone, movement or friendships.
Contempt and humiliation that continue after you have asked them to stop.
You feel afraid of their reaction most of the time.

body: If several of these are true, it is not your fault, and it is not something better behavior on your part can fix. Abuse is a choice made by the person who does it. Leaving can be the most dangerous time with a controlling partner, so it is wise to plan with a support service.

sections.h: Common mistakes when you see red flags

ul: Explaining it away: "They were just stressed" every time.
Waiting for the person from the first months to come back.
Believing that more love or patience will change them.
Hiding problems from friends because you feel embarrassed.
Arguing about whether it "counts" as abuse instead of asking whether you feel safe and respected.

body: Trust what happens over time more than what is said in a single apology.
You can contact a support service even if you are not sure what you are experiencing. They can help you think it through and plan for safety.

body.note: If you are in danger now, contact your local emergency number. In the US, loveisrespect.org (call, text or chat) and thehotline.org offer free, confidential support; elsewhere, contact a domestic-violence helpline or a local service where you live. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a crisis line or emergency services.

faq.q: What are the biggest red flags on a first date?
faq.a: Ignoring your "no", pushing you to drink or go somewhere private, talking with contempt about exes or the waiter, and pressuring you for personal details or a next date before you are ready.
Feeling jealous sometimes is human. It becomes a red flag when it turns into control: checking your phone, limiting who you see, or anger when you spend time with others.

faq.q: Can a relationship with red flags get better?
faq.a: Yellow flags often improve with honest talks. Serious red flags such as violence, threats or ongoing control rarely change without the person taking full responsibility and getting specialist help, and your safety comes first.

faq.q: What are signs of a toxic relationship?
faq.a: Feeling anxious or drained most of the time, being criticized or mocked, constant arguments that never get resolved, and losing contact with the people who support you. Toxic is not a clinical term, but these signs are worth taking seriously.

It is a good sign that you are asking. Look at the table honestly. If you see your own behavior there, you can apologize, change it, and get help from a counsellor or a service for people who want to stop harmful behavior.
